Yeah. That one, yes.

I mean, it’s kind of embarrassing how little it can take sometimes. Like I’ll be doing something—trying to finish a report, checking something on the rig, even just walking to get one specific thing—and a radio chirp happens, or somebody walks past the bay, or I hear part of another conversation, and it’s like my brain just turns its head completely.

And it’s not always even something outside. Sometimes it’s just a thought, like something from a call yesterday pops into my head, and suddenly I’m thinking about that instead of whatever I was actually doing. Then I’ll come back and realize I’ve been standing there with the same thing in my hand, or I’ve opened the same screen twice, or I have to reread what I was working on because I lost the thread.

The frustrating part is getting back on track. It’s not just “oh, distracted, okay, back to it.” Sometimes it feels like I have to rebuild the whole mental setup of what I was doing. Like, where was I, what step was I on, what was I about to do next—and by then something else happens and I’m off again. So, yeah, noises, movement, people talking, random thoughts… they knock me off more than I’d like to admit.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Not always, no. I mean, worry can definitely make anybody feel wound up, I guess, but the keyed-up feeling I’m thinking of doesn’t always feel like anxiety in my head. A lot of times it’s more physical, like my body is just… running too high.

The clearest example is command meetings. Sitting there through the whole thing, staying planted in the chair, trying to look like I’m calmly paying attention—it feels like my engine is revving while the brakes are on. I’ll be sitting there thinking, I need to stand up, I need to walk the bay, I need to go check the rigs, I need to do something with my hands, anything besides just sit here.

And it’s not necessarily because I’m sitting there worried about something specific. Sometimes there’s nothing I’m actively worried about. It’s just this uncomfortable need to move or get up, like staying still takes way more effort than it should. So, yeah, it can happen when I’m worrying, but usually that restless feeling is its own thing.

Yes. That’s actually a pretty common problem for me.

Like if someone at the station gives me three or four things to get done—nothing huge, just normal station responsibilities—I’ll usually start out fine. I’ll jump on the first one and feel like, okay, I’m on it. But then I get pulled into something else, or I notice something that seems like it needs doing right away, or somebody asks me a quick question, and I shift over to that.

Then later I’ll come back around and realize the original thing is just… sitting there unfinished. Like the hose inventory is halfway done, or the equipment checklist is still sitting on the counter with only part of it filled out. And the frustrating thing is, I don’t always even remember stopping it as a decision. It’s more like I started strong, got diverted, and then the task sort of disappeared from the front of my mind until I physically see it again.

So yeah, starting isn’t usually the hard part. Finishing, especially if there are a few responsibilities stacked together, is where it falls apart.

So, yeah, noises, movement, people talking, random thoughts… they knock me off more than I’d like to admit.\n\nDoctor: When you feel keyed up or unable to settle down, does it usually happen because you’re worrying a lot?\n\nPatient: Not always, no. Either way, it’s getting me in trouble there, and that’s what finally made me come in.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually up, wired, or irritable compared with your normal self?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. So when you say unusually up or wired, I’m trying to think if there was a stretch where people would’ve said, “Whoa, this is not you,” and I don’t know. Irritable, sure, I can get irritated, especially when I feel like things are moving too slow, but I don’t know that it comes in episodes or anything. It feels more like just how I am a lot of the time, not like I wake up one week and I’m a completely different guy.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been through or witnessed something at work or elsewhere that still feels traumatic to you?\n\nPatient: I mean… in my line of work, you see stuff. That’s kind of part of the deal, right? Fires, wrecks, people having the worst day of their life, sometimes things you can’t fix no matter how fast you get there.\n\nBut I don’t know that I’d say there’s one specific thing that still feels traumatic in the way people usually mean it. I’m not trying to dodge the question—I just don’t have, like, a single scene that keeps playing in my head that I’d point to and say, “That’s the thing.” There are definitely calls I don’t like thinking about, and some that sit heavier than others, but I guess I’ve always told myself that’s normal for the job.\n\nSo… maybe? But not in a clear way. Nothing I’ve really labeled that way.\n\nDoctor: When you were a kid, were you already the kind of person who felt constantly on the go or unable to sit still?\n\nPatient: Yeah. I mean, according to my mom, absolutely. She’ll tell you I was like this way back in grade school, not just as an adult with a stressful job.\n\nShe says I was always out of my seat, like I just couldn’t stay planted. Teachers would send notes home because I’d be wandering around or talking when I wasn’t supposed to. And I remember some of it too—blurting out answers before they finished asking the question, not because I was trying to be rude, just because it was like the answer was already in my mouth before I could stop it.\n\nAnd the frustrating thing was, I wasn’t dumb. My mom always says, “You were bright enough to do the work,” which somehow makes it worse, honestly. I’d know the material, but I’d lose the homework or forget to turn it in, or it’d be crumpled somewhere in my backpack. So yeah, this wasn’t something that just showed up recently. It was there pretty early.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have trouble sustaining attention on tasks, even when you want to focus?\n\nPatient: Yeah, definitely. That’s actually one of the more frustrating things, because it’s not like I don’t care or I’m not trying.\n\nLike in briefings at work, or even when we’re doing drone training, I’ll start out locked in. First few minutes, I’m following along, looking at the map or the screen, thinking, okay, got it, this matters, pay attention. And then all of a sudden I realize I’ve been staring at the same spot on the map or the monitor and I didn’t actually take in half of what command just said.\n\nIt’s weird because I’m physically there, I’m looking like I’m listening, but my brain kind of… slips off the track. Then I have to piece it together from context or ask somebody afterward, which is embarrassing, especially when it’s something important and I really did want to catch it the first time.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to deal with?\n\nPatient: I don’t know… not in the way I think you mean, maybe.\n\nLike, I worry about normal stuff—work, bills, whether I forgot something I was supposed to do, whether I’m late getting somewhere, that kind of thing. And with my job, there’s always some amount of being alert, I guess. But I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around constantly worrying when nothing’s going on, like just spiraling for no reason.\n\nSometimes my mind is busy, but I don’t know if I’d call it worry exactly. It’s more like I’m thinking about five different things or replaying something I need to get done, and then I realize I’m making myself tense over it. But if you’re asking whether I feel anxious all the time even when there’s no immediate problem… I’m not sure. I haven’t really thought of myself that way.\n\nSo… maybe occasionally, but I wouldn’t say it’s a main thing I’ve noticed.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever gone for several days needing much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve definitely had stretches where I didn’t sleep much because of shifts or calls or just a bad night, but I wouldn’t say I felt full of energy afterward.\n\nUsually if I’m running on less sleep, I feel it. Maybe I can push through because I have to, especially at work, but that’s different from feeling like I don’t need sleep. I’m more likely to be dragging, irritable, or just kind of running on fumes.\n\nSo, several days with barely any sleep and still feeling great or wired in a good way? No, I can’t really think of that happening.\n\nDoctor: Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, paperwork, or equipment?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure how to answer that one cleanly.\n\nI mean… everyone loses their keys sometimes, right? So I don’t know where the line is between normal and “often.” I do have moments where I’m patting all my pockets and checking the counter, the truck, the kitchen, the same two places over and over, but I guess I haven’t kept track of it or thought of it as a main problem.\n\nWith work stuff, I try pretty hard to keep things in the same place because equipment matters, obviously. So I’ve built habits around that, like if something has a spot, I try to put it back there. Paperwork is probably more annoying, but again, I don’t know if that’s me misplacing it or just having too much floating around.\n\nSo… maybe sometimes, but I can’t honestly say, “Yes, all the time,” because I haven’t really paid attention to that specifically.\n\nDoctor: Are you often easily distracted by things going on around you, like noises, movement, or other people talking?\n\nPatient: Yeah. That one, yes.\n\nI mean, it’s kind of embarrassing how little it can take sometimes. Like I’ll be doing something—trying to finish a report, checking something on the rig, even just walking to get one specific thing—and a radio chirp happens, or somebody walks past the bay, or I hear part of another conversation, and it’s like my brain just turns its head completely.\n\nAnd it’s not always even something outside. Sometimes it’s just a thought, like something from a call yesterday pops into my head, and suddenly I’m thinking about that instead of whatever I was actually doing. Then I’ll come back and realize I’ve been standing there with the same thing in my hand, or I’ve opened the same screen twice, or I have to reread what I was working on because I lost the thread.\n\nThe frustrating part is getting back on track. It’s not just “oh, distracted, okay, back to it.” Sometimes it feels like I have to rebuild the whole mental setup of what I was doing. Like, where was I, what step was I on, what was I about to do next—and by then something else happens and I’m off again. So, yeah, noises, movement, people talking, random thoughts… they knock me off more than I’d like to admit.\n\nDoctor: When you feel keyed up or unable to settle down, does it usually happen because you’re worrying a lot?\n\nPatient: Not always, no. I mean, worry can definitely make anybody feel wound up, I guess, but the keyed-up feeling I’m thinking of doesn’t always feel like anxiety in my head. A lot of times it’s more physical, like my body is just… running too high.\n\nThe clearest example is command meetings. Sitting there through the whole thing, staying planted in the chair, trying to look like I’m calmly paying attention—it feels like my engine is revving while the brakes are on. I’ll be sitting there thinking, I need to stand up, I need to walk the bay, I need to go check the rigs, I need to do something with my hands, anything besides just sit here.\n\nAnd it’s not necessarily because I’m sitting there worried about something specific. Sometimes there’s nothing I’m actively worried about. It’s just this uncomfortable need to move or get up, like staying still takes way more effort than it should. So, yeah, it can happen when I’m worrying, but usually that restless feeling is its own thing.\n\nDoctor: Do you often start tasks or responsibilities but have trouble finishing them?\n\nPatient: Yes. That’s actually a pretty common problem for me.\n\nLike if someone at the station gives me three or four things to get done—nothing huge, just normal station responsibilities—I’ll usually start out fine. I’ll jump on the first one and feel like, okay, I’m on it. But then I get pulled into something else, or I notice something that seems like it needs doing right away, or somebody asks me a quick question, and I shift over to that.\n\nThen later I’ll come back around and realize the original thing is just… sitting there unfinished. Like the hose inventory is halfway done, or the equipment checklist is still sitting on the counter with only part of it filled out. And the frustrating thing is, I don’t always even remember stopping it as a decision. It’s more like I started strong, got diverted, and then the task sort of disappeared from the front of my mind until I physically see it again.\n\nSo yeah, starting isn’t usually the hard part. Finishing, especially if there are a few responsibilities stacked together, is where it falls apart.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have trouble organizing tasks and activities?\n\nPatient: I’m not totally sure how to answer that one, honestly. When you say organizing tasks and activities, do you mean like planning out the steps ahead of time, or keeping track of what order things should happen in, or more like keeping my physical stuff organized?\n\nBecause I can think of times where things feel messy in my head, but I don’t know if I’d call it an “organizing” problem exactly without knowing what you mean. It’s not something I’ve really labeled for myself that way. If you mean, like, making a plan and keeping it straight, I’d probably need you to give me an example.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have trouble figuring out the steps of a task and keeping them in order?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t know that I’ve really paid attention to it in that exact way—like “figuring out steps and keeping them in order.”\n\nI mean, with some things, especially things I’ve done a thousand times at work, the steps are just kind of built in, so I’m not sitting there consciously planning them out. I just do them because that’s how we do them. But if you mean more generally, like when something has multiple parts and I have to decide what comes first, what comes next, and not lose the thread… I’d have to think about that.\n\nI can say there are times where a task feels like it has too many moving pieces and I kind of have to talk myself through it or write it down, but I don’t know if that’s what you’re asking. I wouldn’t want to say yes too strongly if I’m misunderstanding you. Could you give me an example of the kind of task you mean?\n\nDoctor: Do these same attention or restlessness problems also cause trouble for you outside of work, like at home or in daily life?\n\nPatient: Yeah, it does, but honestly the place I feel it the most—the place where it’s really starting to matter—is still the firehouse. I know you asked outside of work, and I can answer that, but the work part is what’s been weighing on me because it’s not just annoying anymore. It’s starting to cost me people’s trust.\n\nI got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which was… pretty embarrassing, honestly. Not because I don’t care, because I do care a lot. It’s not like forgetting something small at home where maybe it’s frustrating but nobody gets hurt. At the station, if I miss something or don’t keep track of what I’m supposed to be tracking, it affects how people see me and whether they feel like I’m reliable.\n\nAnd I’ve been wanting to move more toward leadership, or at least be seen as someone who could handle more responsibility, but now it feels like that’s slipping away. I’m not sure I’d describe it as excessive worry about a lot of different areas, no.
